items.title: Chink Martin Interview, 1966-10-19
items.q: Well as a rule, they put Louis Armstrong as king of jazz.

ctx.x: I always felt sorry for the bass player in some of these modern jazz bands because he's the only one that's keeping the tempo. The drummer is playing strictly counterpoint, making bombs bursting in air.

That's right. The bass man is the only one making dum ba dum ba dum. And I will say it brought forth the best of the bass. The drum player is making a ribbit. The bum bing. That's not helping the rhythm at all. Yeah. Oh well. Well, I guess that's it. How were the tempos in the old times? Did they play everything so fast? No, the old tempos was mediocre. That's what I learned. That's mediocre. That's what I want to get into. The same thing. Now the man I spoke to was Sante Piccolo, our trombone player. Well, we…

That's what I was telling you one other time, Tink, you may remember, why I kind of differentiate between what some people think of as Dixieland today and what we think of New Orleans jazz, all this fast stuff that they call Dixieland today, that's what I say, that's the Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey version of New Orleans jazz.
